keyQuotes: Both underdog sides were passive and deliberately so.
Football is a sport of trade-offs.

Tactics can help the smaller nations bridge the gap and play on their own terms but the aura of the World Cup appears to bring out of players a level of performance that they perhaps did not know they possessed.

mainPoints.explanation: Cape Verde and Ghana both used a 4-5-1 with very small gaps between lines; they did not engage when Spain or England dropped deep, denying space in dangerous areas.
mainPoints.point: Compact defensive shape and refusing to be provoked are critical for underdogs.

mainPoints.explanation: Saudi Arabia and Sweden were caught in two-against-one situations on the flanks because their midfield shifted too narrow; switching to a 4-5-1 improved Sweden later.
mainPoints.point: A back five can be a liability if midfielders fail to cover the full width of the pitch.

mainPoints.explanation: Cape Verde, South Africa, and Iraq used big distances between players to force man-for-man pressing, then chipped into space, creating counterattacks despite the risk of losing possession.
mainPoints.point: Short goal-kicks with stretched player positions help underdogs bypass high presses.

mainPoints.explanation: Goalkeepers like Vozinha (Cape Verde) and Eloy Room (Curacao) made record saves, while coherent team structure allowed lesser teams to play on their own terms.
mainPoints.point: Tactical discipline plus inspired individual performances can produce historic results.

oneSentenceSummary: This article uses tactical analysis, statistics, and match examples to explain why lower-ranked teams like Cape Verde, Ghana, and South Africa have earned surprising results at the 2026 World Cup.
originalTitle: World Cup 2026: Why are the underdogs doing so well?
summary: BBC Sport's football tactics correspondent unpacks the common patterns behind the World Cup underdog performances. The piece examines four key themes: refusing to be drawn out of shape (Cape Verde vs Spain, Ghana vs England), covering the pitch widthally (contrasting Saudi Arabia and Sweden's failed back-five systems vs Cape Verde and Ghana's compact 4-5-1), attracting pressure then playing long from short goal-kicks (South Africa vs South Korea, Iraq vs Norway), and acknowledging the role of individual quality and inspired goalkeeping. The analysis uses diagrams, PPDA data, and specific match situations to show how discipline and tactical intelligence can narrow the gap against stronger opponents.
title: World Cup 2026: Why are the underdogs doing so well?
